stem: 2 years old male presented in annual checkup with start to have abnormal fasting glucose result and high blood preesure readings (No numbers just like this) . His BMI is 31 classifying him as obese with history of significant smoking and frequent fast food eating with sedentary lifestyle. LDL:4.03 Total cholesterol: 7.04 What is initial step in managing the patient ?
OptA: Focus in weight loss to reduce BMI.
OptB: Start antihypertensive medication and lipid lowering agent
OptC: smoking cessation , exercise , reduce weight and follow up him
why_right: This young man has a cluster of modifiable risk factors: impaired fasting glucose, high BP readings (not yet confirmed or staged), BMI 31, significant smoking, fast food and a sedentary lifestyle, with raised cholesterol. The lead in asks for the initial step, which is comprehensive lifestyle change addressing every factor (stop smoking, exercise, diet and weight loss) with follow up to recheck BP, glucose and lipids before deciding on drugs.
why_wrong_block:
A. Weight loss is part of the plan but only one item; it ignores smoking, a major modifiable cardiovascular risk factor in this patient. The best answer is the one covering all his risks.
B. Drugs come later: the BP has not been confirmed by repeated readings, and in a young patient without diabetes or established cardiovascular disease an LDL of 4.03 mmol/L is below the very high threshold (4.9 mmol/L, 190 mg/dL) that mandates a statin regardless of risk. Drugs would be right if lifestyle change fails or risk is high on reassessment.
D. Reassurance is wrong because he has several cardiovascular risk factors and prediabetes that need active intervention now; reassurance fits only a fully normal check up.
key_concept:
Metabolic risk cluster on screening: lifestyle first, then reassess.
  • Stop smoking, exercise, diet, weight loss
  • Confirm hypertension on repeated readings before labelling or treating
  • Stage 1 HTN without target organ damage → lifestyle first, drugs if no response
  • Statin regardless of risk: LDL ≥ 4.9 mmol/L (190 mg/dL), diabetes age 40 to 75, clinical ASCVD
exam_pearl: 'Initial step' + several risk factors = the answer that bundles ALL lifestyle measures, not weight loss alone.

stem: A 61-year-old man comes to the clinic with a 2-day history of dyspnoea on exertion. He has a long standing hypertension and a 30-pack-year smoking history. Physical examination is unremarkable except for rare crackles at the bases of the lungs. Which of the following ( something like most specific most helpful in diagnosing )
highlight_terms_source: rare crackles at the bases of the lungs
why_right: A long standing hypertensive smoker with exertional dyspnea and basal crackles is suspected of left ventricular dysfunction (heart failure). BNP (or NT pro BNP) is released by stretched ventricular myocardium, so it is the most helpful blood test to detect ventricular dysfunction; a normal level makes heart failure unlikely. The same applies to the recalled variant (COPD patient with SOB, crackles and leg edema → pro BNP).
why_wrong_block:
B. CRP is a non specific inflammatory marker; it would support pneumonia or another inflammatory process, not ventricular dysfunction.
C. CK (CK MB) is a marker of myocardial injury and ischemia, used for infarction rather than for heart failure.
D. Troponin T marks myocardial necrosis and is the test for acute coronary syndrome (chest pain, ischemic ECG), not the test for ventricular dysfunction.
key_concept:
Cardiac biomarkers by question asked:
  • Ventricular dysfunction / heart failure → BNP or NT pro BNP
  • Myocardial injury / MI → troponin (CK MB older)
  • Inflammation → CRP
  • BNP also raised by: older age, renal failure, ACS, PE, cor pulmonale
  • BNP lower than expected: obesity, flash pulmonary edema, mitral stenosis/acute MR
exam_pearl: Dyspnea + crackles, 'detect LV dysfunction' → BNP; chest pain/ischemia → troponin.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Q: Patient known case of COPD with SOB, crackles and lower limb oedema, most appropriate lab investigation: pro bnp.

stem: 59 years old patient came to ED with fever chils And worsening coough with yellow to greenish phlegm which started 4-5 days before the presentation Patient knows case of COPD DM OA(knee) On examination respiratory distress and crackles in all lungs felid GCS12/15 Chest x ray PA( hyperinflated lung with lower lobe infiltration and air bronchogram ) What the most appropriate next step in management ??? Bp90/50 Hr 128 Rr24 Temp 39 His MAP is 63, Wbs 18k Neutrophil 80% Hg 10.1 Cr 190 (normal up to 115) Lactic acid venous 4 (notmal up to 2) FBG very high ( sorry don't remember) CRP 190
why_right: This is severe community acquired pneumonia with sepsis induced hypoperfusion: fever, purulent sputum, lobar infiltrate with air bronchogram, BP 90/50 (MAP 63), HR 128, lactate 4, raised creatinine and GCS 12. The stem mentions no fluid given yet, so the first step to restore perfusion is IV crystalloid resuscitation; antibiotics and cultures are started in the same first hour, but the immediate threat is circulatory.
why_wrong_block:
B. A vasopressor (norepinephrine) is right when hypotension persists after adequate fluid resuscitation (septic shock). Starting it before any fluid in a volume depleted septic patient is premature.
C. Hb 10.1 is above the usual transfusion threshold of 7 g/dL in sepsis without active bleeding or acute coronary ischemia, so transfusion is not indicated.
D. Antibiotics are essential and must be given within the first hour, alongside fluids, after cultures. When the question asks for the single next step in a hypotensive, hypoperfused patient, circulation (fluids) is prioritised; antibiotics would be the answer if the patient were hemodynamically stable.
key_concept:
Sepsis first hour bundle: hypotension or lactate ≥ 4 → fluids now.
  • Measure lactate, blood cultures before antibiotics
  • Broad spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour
  • Crystalloid resuscitation for hypotension or high lactate
  • Vasopressor (norepinephrine) if MAP stays < 65 after fluids
  • Transfuse only if Hb < 7 g/dL (no bleeding or ischemia)
exam_pearl: No fluid given yet → fluids; BP still low after fluids → vasopressor (compare the norepinephrine card).
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other recalled versions (unmarked): elderly DM/OA patient with fever, chills, yellowish green phlegm, respiratory distress, GCS 12/15, Hb 10.6, hypotension (90s/60s), left lower infiltration with air bronchogram; options Vasopressor / Give antibiotic(s) / Blood transfusion / Fluid resuscitation. Also: 55y with 5 day SOB, pneumonia, BP 90/70, HR 123, SpO2 95 on 3L, Temp 38; options Vasopressor / IV Fluid / ABx / Antipyretics.

stem: COPD AND HAVE ACIDOSIS WHAT IS THE INITIAL INVESTIGATION
why_right: A COPD patient with acidosis (respiratory acidosis already shown on the blood gas) is having an acute exacerbation with ventilatory failure. The initial investigation is a chest X-ray to find the trigger or complication that changes management: pneumonia, pneumothorax, pulmonary edema or effusion. It is quick, bedside and done in every admitted exacerbation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Contrast CT is not an initial test in COPD exacerbation; CT pulmonary angiography is reserved for suspected PE after initial assessment, and it delays care in an acidotic patient.
C. CBC is part of routine admission bloods (white count, polycythemia, anemia) but it is supportive and does not identify the precipitant the way a chest X-ray does.
D. Sputum culture is sent when sputum is purulent or the patient is admitted, to guide antibiotics, but results are delayed and it is not the initial investigation.
key_concept:
Acute COPD exacerbation work up:
  • ABG: defines respiratory acidosis and need for NIV
  • Chest X-ray: pneumonia, pneumothorax, edema, effusion
  • ECG, CBC, electrolytes; sputum culture if purulent
  • pH < 7.35 with high PaCO2 despite treatment → NIV (BiPAP)
  • CT only for specific questions (e.g. suspected PE)
exam_pearl: Acidosis already known → next/initial investigation is the CXR to find the trigger.

stem: 40 years old famle came to follow up clinic , she was in good health 2 years old when examined Past medical hx of Rheumatic fever 15 years ago she smokes 10 cigarettes for 15 years On current examination she have good heart rhythm and blowing Diastolic decrescendo murmur at aortic area BP 154/56 HR 68 What the most appropriate advice for future preventive health maintenance ?
OptD: prophylaxis Abx before the dental procedure
highlight_terms_source: blowing Diastolic decrescendo murmur at aortic area
why_right: The "blowing diastolic decrescendo murmur at the aortic area" with a wide pulse pressure (BP 154/56) after "rheumatic fever 15 years ago" points to rheumatic aortic regurgitation. A newly heard valvular murmur must first be characterised by transthoracic echo, which shows severity, LV size and EF, and decides surveillance or surgery timing. Every later preventive decision for this valve depends on that echo, so it is the key step here.
why_wrong_block:
A. An annual chest X ray is not a screening or surveillance tool for valve disease or for smokers; it cannot grade the regurgitation or LV function. Lung cancer screening, when indicated, uses low dose CT in older heavy smokers.
B. Colorectal screening is not the issue raised by this vignette, and an annual flexible sigmoidoscopy is not a recommended interval. It would be right only for a colorectal screening question at screening age.
D. Native valve disease from rheumatic heart disease without prior endocarditis is not an indication for dental antibiotic prophylaxis under current guidance. It is reserved for prosthetic valves, previous infective endocarditis, certain congenital heart disease and cardiac transplant valvulopathy.
key_concept:
New murmur = transthoracic echo first.
  • Diastolic decrescendo murmur at aortic area + wide pulse pressure = aortic regurgitation.
  • TTE: first test for a murmur; TEE gives better detail when needed.
  • Asymptomatic valve disease: follow up and medical treatment; symptomatic or low EF: surgery.
  • Dental prophylaxis: prosthetic valve, prior IE, selected congenital disease only.
  • Rheumatic carditis with residual valve disease: secondary prophylaxis for 10 years after last attack or until age 40, whichever is longer.
exam_pearl: Rheumatic valve disease alone does not earn dental prophylaxis; prosthetic valve or prior endocarditis does.

stem: 28-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 2-week history of bloody diarrhea, lower abdominal cramps, and tenesmus. Physical examination reveals abdominal distension with mild tenderness (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to establish the diagnosis?
why_right: A 28 year old with 2 weeks of bloody diarrhea, cramps and tenesmus has a subacute colitis picture typical of ulcerative colitis (tenesmus reflects rectal involvement). The lead in asks for the investigation that establishes the diagnosis: colonoscopy with biopsy shows continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum and gives histology to confirm UC.
why_wrong_block:
B. CT shows bowel wall thickening and complications (perforation, toxic megacolon, abscess) but cannot confirm mucosal disease or give histology.
C. C. difficile toxin testing is for diarrhea after antibiotics or hospitalization (or a flare in known IBD); no such exposure is given here, and it does not diagnose UC.
D. Stool culture is done to exclude infective colitis, but a negative culture only rules out infection; it does not establish the diagnosis.
key_concept:
Suspected IBD: stool studies exclude infection, colonoscopy with biopsy confirms.
  • UC: continuous from rectum, bloody diarrhea, tenesmus, mucosal disease
  • Crohn: skip lesions, transmural, terminal ileum, fistulas
  • CT: complications or severe disease
  • Severe colitis or suspected toxic megacolon: avoid full colonoscopy, use flexible sigmoidoscopy and X-ray or CT
exam_pearl: If the stem adds fever, tachycardia and marked colonic dilatation (toxic megacolon), full colonoscopy becomes dangerous; none of these is described here.

stem: A 22-year-old man presented to the Emergency Room with left leg swelling and pain that started 2 days ago and is getting worse. It involves the whole left leg. He also complains of chest tightness and shortness of breath. Examination reveals left lower limb pitting edema extending to the thigh (see report). ECG: Sinus tachycardia. Which of the following is the most appropriate management at this time?
highlight_terms_source: chest tightness and shortness of breath
why_right: Whole left leg swelling to the thigh is a proximal DVT, and new chest tightness, dyspnea and sinus tachycardia indicate it has embolized (PE). In a stable patient the immediate step is parenteral anticoagulation; LMWH is first line, and when it is not offered, unfractionated heparin is the correct choice "at this time".
why_wrong_block:
A. Aspirin: an antiplatelet; it has no role in treating venous thromboembolism, which is fibrin rich clot needing anticoagulation.
B. Clopidogrel: also an antiplatelet, used for arterial disease (ACS, stents, stroke), not DVT or PE.
C. Warfarin: used for longer term anticoagulation and must overlap with heparin; started alone it is slow and briefly prothrombotic.
key_concept:
VTE management ladder:
  • Stable DVT or PE: LMWH first line (or DOAC); UFH if LMWH not offered or renal failure or possible thrombolysis
  • Warfarin: start with heparin overlap until INR therapeutic
  • Unstable (hypotension) PE: thrombolysis
  • Anticoagulation contraindicated: IVC filter
exam_pearl: "At this time" asks for the acute agent: heparin, never warfarin alone and never an antiplatelet.

stem: 71-year-old man is evaluated after a recent hospitalization 10 days ago for pneumonia and was discharged with a 10-day course of appropriate antibiotics. For the past 5 days, he has had a low-grade fever and increased shortness of breath. Pulmonary examination reveals decreased fremitus, dullness to percussion, and decreased breath sounds over the lower third of the right hemithorax (see lab results and report). Chest radiograph: Moderate right-sided pleural effusion. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: recent hospitalization 10 days ago for pneumonia
why_right: He was "hospitalized 10 days ago for pneumonia" and now has "low-grade fever and increased shortness of breath" with a moderate effusion, so this is hospital acquired infection complicated by a parapneumonic effusion or empyema. Piperacillin-tazobactam covers Pseudomonas and other hospital organisms, and the infected fluid must be drained for source control.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ceftriaxone + azithromycin is a community acquired pneumonia regimen, and it leaves the infected effusion undrained. Right for a fresh CAP admission without recent hospitalisation.
B. Drainage is correct, but levofloxacin alone is a weaker choice: it gives unreliable anaerobic cover for an infected effusion or empyema, and he has just finished an antibiotic course, so resistance is likely. Piperacillin-tazobactam covers Pseudomonas, gram negatives and anaerobes in one agent.
C. Watchful waiting is unsafe with fever, worsening breathlessness and a moderate effusion suggesting a complicated parapneumonic effusion. A repeat film is for a resolving, asymptomatic simple effusion.
key_concept:
Post-hospital pneumonia + effusion = drain + antipseudomonal antibiotic.
  • Hospital acquired pneumonia: onset 48 to 72 hours or more after admission.
  • Cover Pseudomonas: piperacillin-tazobactam.
  • CAP regimens (ceftriaxone + azithromycin, levofloxacin) are inadequate here.
  • Infected/complicated effusion or empyema: drain (small-bore drain or chest tube).
exam_pearl: "Hospitalized recently" is the clue that turns a CAP regimen into a wrong answer.

stem: A 71-year-old man is evaluated after a recent hospitalization 10 days ago for pneumonia and was discharged with a 10-day course of appropriate antibiotics. For the past 5 days, he has had a low-grade fever and increased shortness of breath. Pulmonary examination reveals decreased fremitus, dullness to percussion, and decreased breath sounds over the lower third of the right hemithorax (see lab results and report). Chest radiograph: Moderate right-sided pleural effusion. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: recent hospitalization 10 days ago for pneumonia
why_right: Fever and dyspnea starting days after discharge from a pneumonia admission, with dullness, reduced fremitus and a "moderate right-sided pleural effusion", point to a complicated parapneumonic effusion or empyema in a recently hospitalized patient. Infected pleural fluid must be drained, and a small-bore drain is adequate for most such collections. Because he was recently in hospital and already had a full antibiotic course, empiric cover must be broad (Pseudomonas, resistant gram-negatives and anaerobes), which piperacillin-tazobactam provides.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is a community-acquired pneumonia regimen; it lacks antipseudomonal cover after recent hospitalization and does not drain the infected effusion.
B. Drainage is right, but levofloxacin is a community-acquired pneumonia agent here: it lacks reliable anaerobic cover for a pleural infection after recent hospitalization and antibiotics; a large-bore chest tube is also not needed when a small-bore drain usually suffices.
C. Watchful waiting suits a small, resolving effusion in a well patient; persistent fever with a moderate effusion after pneumonia needs drainage and antibiotics now.
key_concept:
Pneumonia plus effusion that fails to settle: drain the pleural space and give antibiotics suited to where the infection was acquired.
  • New effusion with pneumonia: diagnostic thoracentesis first
  • Pus, positive Gram stain/culture, or complicated fluid: drain (small-bore tube usually enough)
  • Community-acquired: ceftriaxone plus azithromycin
  • Hospital-acquired or recent admission/antibiotics: antipseudomonal agent (e.g. piperacillin-tazobactam)
exam_pearl: Recent hospital stay + fever + effusion = drain it and cover Pseudomonas; antibiotics alone or a CAP regimen are traps.

stem: Female pt k/c of COPD presented with hepatomegaly, increasing SOB, +ve shifting dullness, LL edema and raised JVP with giant 'a' wave (I am not sure but I think also there is finding in heart auscultation). What is causing these symptoms?
why_right: In a "k/c of COPD" patient, raised JVP, hepatomegaly, ascites and leg edema are systemic venous congestion, the picture of right heart failure. Chronic hypoxic lung disease causes pulmonary hypertension and then right ventricular failure (cor pulmonale). A giant a wave reflects the stiff, hypertrophied right ventricle that the right atrium must push against.
why_wrong_block:
B. Left heart failure presents with pulmonary congestion: orthopnea, PND, basal crackles, S3. It is right only when those findings dominate; here the findings are systemic congestion in a COPD patient.
C. Chronic liver disease gives ascites and edema but a normal or low JVP and stigmata of liver disease. A raised JVP with giant a wave points to the heart, not the liver.
key_concept:
COPD + raised JVP + hepatomegaly + edema = cor pulmonale (right heart failure).
  • Pulmonary hypertension sign: loud P2, parasternal heave.
  • Giant a wave: RV hypertrophy/pulmonary hypertension or tricuspid stenosis.
  • Giant v wave: tricuspid regurgitation; cannon a waves: complete heart block; absent a: AF.
  • Next step for suspected cor pulmonale: echocardiogram.
  • Raised JVP separates cardiac ascites from cirrhosis.
exam_pearl: Ascites with a RAISED JVP is cardiac; ascites with a normal JVP is liver.

stem: Case of a woman in her 30's presenting with shortness of breath and chest pain for one day. There is no cough or fever, vitally stable, labs all normal except D dimer 800 high. ECG showed peaked P wave in lead II and right deviation with right bundle branch block. What is the most helpful investigation to be done?
highlight_terms_source: shortness of breath and chest pain for one day
right deviation with right bundle branch block
why_right: Sudden "shortness of breath and chest pain" with no cough or fever, a raised D dimer, and ECG right heart strain (peaked P in II, right axis deviation, RBBB) make pulmonary embolism the working diagnosis. She is "vitally stable", so she can go to CT, and CT pulmonary angiography is the test that confirms the diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Echo shows only indirect signs (RV strain) and cannot confirm PE. It is the choice in a hemodynamically unstable patient who cannot be moved to CT.
B. A V/Q scan is used when CT contrast is contraindicated (renal impairment, contrast allergy), in pregnancy, when CTPA is inconclusive, or for chronic PE. None applies here.
D. MR angiography is not a standard first line test for PE; it is less sensitive and less available than CTPA.
key_concept:
Stable suspected PE with raised D dimer = CT pulmonary angiography.
  • D dimer: rules out PE only when negative in low probability; cannot confirm.
  • ECG: sinus tachycardia (commonest), S1Q3T3, RBBB, right axis, P pulmonale.
  • Unstable PE: bedside echo.
  • V/Q: contrast contraindicated, pregnancy, inconclusive CT, chronic PE.
exam_pearl: "Vitally stable" sends her to CTPA; hypotension would switch the answer to bedside echo.

stem: 51 yo pt, k/c of DM, HTN, renal impairment 3, compliant on his medications. Diagnosed as AF and the physician decides to give him anticoagulant, what is the best to add?
why_right: With HTN and DM he already scores at least 2 on CHA2DS2-VA, so anticoagulation is indicated, and DOACs are first line. The decisive clue is "renal impairment 3": among the DOACs apixaban depends least on renal clearance and has the most favourable bleeding and safety data in CKD, so it is the best choice.
why_wrong_block:
B. Rivaroxaban is a reasonable DOAC but is more renally cleared than apixaban and needs dose reduction in moderate CKD. Right for a patient with normal renal function who prefers once daily dosing.
C. Dabigatran is mostly renally excreted, so it accumulates and raises bleeding risk in CKD. It suits patients with good renal function.
D. Edoxaban also needs renal dose adjustment and has reduced efficacy at very high creatinine clearance. It is not the preferred agent when renal function is the issue.
key_concept:
AF anticoagulation in CKD: apixaban is the DOAC least dependent on the kidney.
  • Anticoagulate when CHA2DS2-VA is 2 or more.
  • First line: DOAC; warfarin (INR 2 to 3) for mechanical valve or moderate/severe mitral stenosis.
  • Renal dependence: dabigatran highest, apixaban lowest.
  • Severe renal failure/dialysis: warfarin is the traditional choice.
exam_pearl: Kidney in the stem = avoid dabigatran, pick apixaban.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler added a 'Q:' variant: 'Female known case of A-fib, it was decided she start anticoagulation. What is the most appropriate? a-Apixaban b-Rivaroxaban c-Edoxaban d-Dabigatran' (unmarked).

stem: 45 k/c of HTN and 20 pack smoker, BMI 28, asymptomatic, came for check up. Best prevention for patient care? BP 150/95. Labs: HDL 1.1, LDL 4.5, Cholesterol 6.5, Triglycerides 2.1.
OptD: Lifestyle modification and follow up in 3 months
why_right: He is a "k/c of HTN" whose BP is still 150/95, and he also smokes and has LDL 4.5 mmol/L, so his cardiovascular risk is high and both factors need drug treatment. Antihypertensive therapy plus a statin is the preventive step that lowers his risk, alongside smoking cessation and lifestyle advice.
why_wrong_block:
A. Stress testing is not a screening test in an asymptomatic person; it is used to investigate exertional chest pain or other ischemic symptoms.
B. Option not recalled, so it cannot be judged.
D. Lifestyle alone with review is for newly found mild hypertension in a low risk patient without other risk factors. Here he is already hypertensive, uncontrolled, a smoker and has high LDL, so delaying drugs is inadequate.
key_concept:
Multiple risk factors + uncontrolled BP + high LDL = drug therapy for both, plus lifestyle.
  • Mild, newly found BP in a low risk patient: lifestyle first, then drugs if no response.
  • Known HTN not at target: start or step up antihypertensives.
  • Raised LDL with smoking and HTN: statin.
  • Smoking cessation is part of every answer.
  • Stress test is not for asymptomatic screening.
exam_pearl: "Known case" of HTN with BP still high is not a lifestyle only question.

stem: A 24-year-old woman is reviewed in the Asthma Clinic. She currently uses a salbutamol inhaler 100 mcg prn combined with a beclometasone dipropionate inhaler 400 mcg bd. Despite this, she is having frequent exacerbations of her asthma that required frequent courses of prednisolone and hospitalization three times in the last 6 months. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
OptB: Start to take the salbutamol regularly
why_right: She is already on a reliever plus a regular inhaled glucocorticoid (beclometasone 400 mcg twice daily), yet has "frequent exacerbations", repeated prednisolone courses and three admissions in 6 months. Her asthma is uncontrolled on ICS, so treatment must be stepped up. The next step is to add a LABA such as salmeterol to the ICS (ideally as a combination inhaler), assuming adherence and technique are checked.
why_wrong_block:
A. Switching beclometasone to fluticasone swaps one ICS for another and is not a step up; it would only matter for intolerance or device issues.
B. Regular salbutamol does not treat inflammation, and rising reliever use is itself a sign of poor control, not a treatment.
D. Tiotropium (LAMA) is an add-on for asthma still uncontrolled on ICS plus LABA, not the first add-on after ICS alone.
key_concept:
Uncontrolled on ICS: add a LABA before anything else.
  • Step 1: as-needed reliever
  • Step 2: low-dose ICS
  • Step 3: ICS plus LABA
  • Step 4: higher-dose ICS or add leukotriene antagonist or LAMA
  • Step 5: specialist, biologics or oral steroids
  • Always check adherence and inhaler technique before stepping up
exam_pearl: LABA is the first add-on to ICS; tiotropium comes only after ICS plus LABA fails.

stem: COPD exacerbation, after viral infection and runny nose. After stabilizing the patient and giving steroid, salbutamol and sending septic screen: BP 140/80s, O2 70%, CO2 high 9, pH 7.2. X ray given (showed loss of sharpness in costophrenic angle, looks overloaded). What is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: Despite steroid and bronchodilators he has life threatening ventilatory failure: "O2 70%", CO2 9 and pH 7.2. The rule used in these recalls is that in COPD a pH below 7.25 means intubate, while a milder acidosis gets NIV. The only alternative offered is negative pressure ventilation, which is not a standard therapy, so intubation and mechanical ventilation is the answer.
why_wrong_block: B. Negative pressure ventilation (cuirass or iron lung) is not used for acute COPD exacerbations. The non invasive option that is right is POSITIVE pressure (BiPAP), for an alert patient with milder acidosis.
key_concept:
Acute COPD ventilation ladder.
  • Controlled oxygen via Venturi, target SpO2 88 to 92%.
  • NIV (BiPAP): alert, cooperative, hypercapnic acidosis despite medical therapy.
  • Intubate: reduced consciousness, aspiration risk/secretions, NIV failure, severe hypoxemia or deep acidosis.
  • Recall rule: COPD pH <7.25 intubate; pH above 7.25 NIV (non COPD: <7.15).
  • Real guidelines still allow a closely monitored NIV trial in ICU below 7.25 if alert; the cut off is the exam rule.
exam_pearl: The same stem at pH 7.27 with a clear sensorium flips to positive pressure NIV (see 1381B).
compiler_note: Compiler note: Typed options unmarked. Embedded Alhomrani screenshot: new recall with same stem, conscious alert, but pH <7.25: Answer: Elective Intubation (PROBABLY confirmed). Rule: pH <7.25: intubate; pH >7.25: positive pressure. In COPD intubate if pH <7.25; in non-COPD intubate if pH <7.15. See 1381b for the pH 7.24/7.27 version (Answer B, positive pressure).

stem: A patient with acute exacerbation COPD; they literally gave him everything for management of COPD (Nebs, SABA, SAMA, ABX) but no O2 given. He does not have confusion or any CNS symptoms or absent gag or any indication for intubation. ABG: CO2 high, O2 low, pH 7.24 (hand-corrected to 7.27), O2 sat 70%.
highlight_terms_source: not have confusion or any CNS symptoms or absent gag or any indication for intubation
why_right: He has hypercapnic respiratory acidosis (pH 7.27, high CO2) despite full medical therapy, but "no confusion or any CNS symptoms or absent gag". An alert patient with intact airway reflexes and acidosis above the intubation threshold meets the criteria for non invasive positive pressure ventilation (BiPAP), given with controlled oxygen.
why_wrong_block:
A. High flow nasal cannula mainly treats hypoxemia and does not reliably correct hypercapnic acidosis. It may be used if NIV is not tolerated, not as first choice here.
C. Intubation needs a reason: reduced consciousness, aspiration risk, NIV failure or severe acidosis (pH <7.25 in these recalls). The stem explicitly excludes all of them.
key_concept:
Alert COPD patient + hypercapnic acidosis despite treatment = NIV.
  • NIV criteria: alert/cooperative, distress despite bronchodilators and steroids, hypercapnia with acidosis.
  • Oxygen: Venturi, target 88 to 92%.
  • Intubate: drowsy, secretions/absent gag, NIV failure, pH <7.25 (recall rule).
exam_pearl: The handwritten change from pH 7.24 to 7.27 is the whole question: above 7.25 and alert = NIV.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot within 1381: B circled by pen and 'Answer: B' printed; pH 7.24 crossed out and handwritten 7.27. Alhomrani: this is my recall; everything in red is my own words; honestly I don't think his pH was 7.24. In COPD intubate if pH <7.25; non-COPD if pH <7.15.

stem: A 20-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Room with a 2-day history of headache, fever, photosensitivity, lethargy, and skin eruption. Her examination reveals a drowsy woman with neck rigidity but no focal neurological findings. She has a purpuric skin rash over her extremities (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to establish the diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: purpuric skin rash over her extremities
why_right: "Headache, fever, photosensitivity, lethargy", "neck rigidity" and a "purpuric skin rash" indicate meningococcal meningitis. There are "no focal neurological findings", and drowsiness alone without papilledema or a markedly reduced level of consciousness does not require CT first, so lumbar puncture, which gives CSF for cell count, glucose, protein, Gram stain and culture, is the investigation that establishes the diagnosis. Blood cultures and empiric antibiotics should be given without waiting for the LP.
why_wrong_block:
A. A biopsy of the purpuric lesions can show organisms but is not the standard test to establish meningitis.
B. Blood cultures should be taken (before antibiotics) but they diagnose bacteremia, not meningeal infection; CSF is what confirms meningitis.
D. Meningococcal serology is slow and has no role in acute diagnosis.
key_concept:
Suspected bacterial meningitis: blood cultures, then LP; do not delay antibiotics.
  • CT before LP only if: focal deficit, papilledema, new seizure, moderate to severe impairment of consciousness, immunocompromise
  • Mild drowsiness or lethargy alone: proceed to LP
  • Bacterial CSF: high neutrophils, low glucose, high protein
  • Purpuric or petechial rash: think meningococcus
  • Antibiotics should not wait for LP if it will be delayed
exam_pearl: If the stem adds a focal deficit or papilledema, CT comes before LP; here "no focal neurological findings" makes LP the answer.

stem: A 30 years old male with 4 month epigastric pain worse after meal. No family history of gastric and esophageal cancer. BMI 35. What is the next step?
why_right: A "30 years old" man with dyspepsia, "no family history of gastric and esophageal cancer" and no alarm features (no weight loss, bleeding, anemia, dysphagia or vomiting) is managed by test and treat. Non invasive H. pylori testing (urea breath test or stool antigen) is the next step; the BMI of 35 is a distractor, not an alarm sign.
why_wrong_block:
B. Endoscopy is for alarm features, older age, family history of upper GI cancer, or failed empirical treatment. Right when the stem adds anemia, bleeding, weight loss or dysphagia.
C. CT abdomen does not show mucosal disease; it is used for suspected complications such as perforation or for other diagnoses.
D. Barium studies are used only when endoscopy is contraindicated or unavailable; they are not part of first line dyspepsia workup.
key_concept:
Young dyspeptic with no alarm features = test and treat H. pylori.
  • Alarm features: weight loss, GI bleeding/anemia, dysphagia, persistent vomiting, family history of upper GI cancer, older age.
  • Any alarm feature: upper endoscopy.
  • Pain worse with meals suggests gastric ulcer; relieved by meals suggests duodenal ulcer.
  • Isolated high urea with low Hb suggests upper GI bleeding: endoscopy.
exam_pearl: Add anemia or weight loss to this stem and the answer flips to endoscopy.

stem: A 25-year-old college student came for a routine checkup. He does not have any active complaints. Examination reveals a diastolic murmur heard at the base of the heart, which increased when the patient leaned forward in full expiration. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: diastolic murmur heard at the base of the heart
increased when the patient leaned forward in full expiration
why_right: The first step with any murmur is timing: this one is diastolic. A diastolic murmur at the base that gets louder when leaning forward in full expiration is the classic early diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation. It is the only diastolic lesion among the options.
why_wrong_block:
A. Aortic stenosis is an ejection systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids.
B. Mitral regurgitation is a pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla.
D. Tricuspid regurgitation is a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge that increases with inspiration.
key_concept:
Decide systolic vs diastolic first.
  • Diastolic (ARMS): aortic regurgitation, mitral stenosis
  • Systolic (MRAS): mitral regurgitation, aortic stenosis
  • AR: early diastolic, base/left sternal edge, louder sitting forward in expiration, wide pulse pressure, collapsing pulse
  • MS: mid diastolic rumble at apex, louder in left lateral position
  • Right sided murmurs (TR, PR) increase with inspiration
exam_pearl: Early diastolic murmur at the base that increases with inspiration rather than expiration is pulmonary regurgitation, not AR.

stem: A 50-year-old man with ischemic heart disease and diabetes presented to the emergency with severe pneumonia and was admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU). He was treated with a course of antibiotics. Three days after admission to ICU, he develops hypotension treated with hydration and inotropes. His liver function at the day of admission was normal, but the repeated one is abnormal (see lab results and report). Abdominal ultrasound: Unremarkable. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: hypotension treated with hydration and inotropes
why_right: LFTs were normal on admission, then he had hypotension needing inotropes on day 3, and the repeat LFTs became abnormal with an unremarkable ultrasound. Reduced hepatic perfusion in a patient with ischemic heart disease causes ischemic (shock) liver: a sudden, marked rise in AST and ALT (often above 1000) shortly after the hypotensive episode, falling quickly once perfusion is restored.
why_wrong_block:
B. ICU (sepsis related) cholestasis gives a mainly raised bilirubin and ALP pattern with only modest transaminases, not a massive AST/ALT surge right after hypotension.
C. Intravascular hemolysis raises unconjugated bilirubin and LDH with falling hemoglobin, but it does not cause a large rise in ALT.
D. Acalculous cholecystitis occurs in critically ill patients but shows fever, RUQ pain and a thick walled distended gallbladder with pericholecystic fluid; the ultrasound here is normal.
key_concept:
Normal LFTs, then hypotension, then very high AST/ALT = ischemic hepatitis.
  • Transaminases often >1000, rising within 24 to 48 h of the insult
  • LDH markedly raised; rapid fall after perfusion restored
  • Risk: heart failure, IHD, shock, sepsis
  • Treatment: restore perfusion, treat the cause
exam_pearl: Time the LFT rise against the hypotensive episode: a sharp rise right after shock is ischemia, not drugs or cholestasis.

stem: A 65-year-old woman presented with a 4-month history of progressive shortness of breath, dry cough, and fatigue. She was treated for pneumonia with 2 courses of antibiotics but showed no improvement in her symptoms. She has no significant medical problems (see reports). Chest X-ray (after antibiotics): A persistent dense area of consolidation at the right lower lobe. Bronchioalveolar lavage: Atypical cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: 4-month history of progressive shortness of breath, dry cough
why_right: A 65-year-old with "4-month" progressive dyspnea, dry cough and fatigue, and a "persistent dense consolidation" that did not resolve after "2 courses of antibiotics", has non-resolving pneumonia, which in an older adult means malignancy (or TB) until proven otherwise. "Atypical cells" on bronchoalveolar lavage confirm a malignant process, so the diagnosis is bronchogenic cancer.
why_wrong_block:
A. Sarcoidosis gives bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with noncaseating granulomas, often in younger patients with erythema nodosum, not a single lobar mass with atypical cells.
B. Atypical pneumonia causes diffuse interstitial infiltrates and responds to macrolides; it does not produce malignant cells or a lobar density persisting for months.
C. Allergic (hypersensitivity) pneumonitis needs an antigen exposure (birds, mould, farming) and shows lymphocytosis on lavage, not atypical cells.
key_concept:
Non-resolving pneumonia in an older patient: think cancer or TB.
  • Persistent consolidation after antibiotics: CT chest and bronchoscopy
  • Atypical cells on BAL or cytology: malignancy
  • Night sweats, hemoptysis, upper lobe cavity: TB
  • Recurrent pneumonia in the same lobe: obstructing lesion
exam_pearl: Same lobe still opaque after antibiotics in a 60+ patient: look for an obstructing tumour.

stem: A young man with HIV was admitted to the Intensive Care Unit with progressive shortness of breath, cough, and fever. Examination showed he was dyspneic and cyanosed (see report). Chest X-ray: Signs of ARDS. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
why_right: The decisive clues are HIV with a progressive (subacute) course of dyspnea, cough and fever, marked hypoxia ("cyanosed") and a diffuse ARDS-like chest X-ray. This is the classic picture of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, the most common opportunistic pneumonia when the CD4 count is below 200. PCP typically gives bilateral interstitial (ground glass) infiltrates with hypoxia out of proportion to the examination, rather than a single lobar consolidation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Staph aureus pneumonia classically follows influenza or another viral URTI (or IV drug use) and tends to be necrotizing or cavitating; nothing here points to a preceding flu illness.
C. Pseudomonas is the typical organism of hospital acquired or ventilator pneumonia, cystic fibrosis and bronchiectasis; this patient arrived with the illness from the community.
D. Strep pneumoniae is the commonest CAP organism overall and in HIV with CD4 above 200, but it presents acutely with lobar consolidation, not a progressive diffuse ARDS picture in advanced HIV.
key_concept:
Pneumonia organism by setting:
  • HIV, CD4 <200, subacute dyspnea, bilateral interstitial infiltrates, hypoxia: Pneumocystis jirovecii
  • HIV with CD4 >200 or healthy adult, acute lobar consolidation: Strep pneumoniae
  • After influenza, cavitating: Staph aureus
  • Hospital acquired, ventilated, CF or bronchiectasis: Pseudomonas
  • PCP clues: high LDH, exertional desaturation; treat with high dose co-trimoxazole, add steroids if severely hypoxic
  • Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis when CD4 <200
exam_pearl: "HIV + progressive breathlessness + diffuse bilateral picture" = PCP; the same patient with abrupt lobar consolidation and high CD4 = pneumococcus.

stem: A 51-year-old patient presents with cough, fever, and lung consolidation. Laboratory results show neutrophilia. No other medical comorbidities. What is the most likely causative organism?
key_concept:
CAP organism by host:
  • Healthy adult, lobar consolidation, neutrophilia: Strep pneumoniae
  • Post influenza or IV drug use: Staph aureus
  • Dry cough, bilateral interstitial infiltrates: atypicals (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, viruses)
  • Hospital acquired: Pseudomonas and gram-negatives
  • Foul sputum, aspiration risk: anaerobes
exam_pearl: "No comorbidities" plus lobar consolidation points away from the special-host organisms; the host and setting decide the organism.

stem: A 45-year-old man was recently diagnosed with hypertension. He has a family history of ischemic heart disease. An angiotensin receptor II blocker was prescribed to control his blood pressure and reduce the risk of ischemic heart disease. Which of the following is the most likely prescribed agent?
why_right: The stem names the class: an angiotensin II receptor blocker. Irbesartan carries the "-sartan" suffix that identifies ARBs, so it is the prescribed agent.
why_wrong_block:
A. Carvedilol is a beta blocker (with alpha blocking action), useful in heart failure, not an ARB.
C. Perindopril is an ACE inhibitor ("-pril"); it acts on the same system but blocks angiotensin II formation, not its receptor.
D. Amiodarone is a class III antiarrhythmic, not an antihypertensive or ARB.
key_concept:
Recognize drug class by suffix.
  • -sartan: ARB (losartan, irbesartan, valsartan)
  • -pril: ACE inhibitor (perindopril, lisinopril)
  • -olol / -ilol: beta blocker (carvedilol)
  • -dipine: dihydropyridine CCB
exam_pearl: Do not confuse ACE inhibitor (-pril, causes dry cough) with ARB (-sartan, no bradykinin cough).
compiler_note: Compiler note: Typed recall: 'Q about patient prescribed ARB. What is this Med? - irbesartan (it was the only ARB in options)'. Screenshot 0144 shows full question with Answer: B.

stem: In a patient with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), what treatment is recommended in addition for remission and to reduce vascular complications?
highlight_terms_source: in addition for remission and to reduce vascular complications
key_concept:
SLE treatment ladder:
  • All patients: hydroxychloroquine (cornerstone)
  • Mild to moderate step 1: hydroxychloroquine + NSAID
  • Step 2: low dose steroid + hydroxychloroquine + methotrexate
  • Life-threatening: high dose steroid + immunosuppressant
  • Neuropsychiatric lupus: cyclophosphamide
  • Lupus nephritis: mycophenolate mofetil
exam_pearl: "Every lupus patient / maintain remission" points to hydroxychloroquine; "seizures or brain lesions" points to cyclophosphamide.

stem: 72 yrs old mal retired free medical hx experience misbalance and i think fall" hx of osteoarthritis in his knee: he want to prevent fall and strengthen his muscle Advice him which type of exercise?
OptB: Low speed walk with swimming aerobic
highlight_terms_source: prevent fall and strengthen his muscle
key_concept:
Exercise in elderly OA and fall risk:
  • Prefer low impact: walking, swimming, water aerobics, cycling
  • Add muscle strengthening (especially quadriceps) and balance training
  • Avoid high impact: running, jumping
  • Weight loss helps knee and hip OA
  • Inactivity worsens deconditioning and fall risk
exam_pearl: In OA and fall risk the answer is almost always the low impact option; "high speed" or "running" is the trap.

stem: Question about old female previously physician, she want to stay active but she is afraid of falling, she suffer from osteoartheritis, whats your recommendation for her
OptB: low impact exercises like walking and aerobic water excersie
OptC: high impact exercises like jumping and running
highlight_terms_source: stay active but she is afraid of falling
why_right: She has osteoarthritis, wants to stay active, and is afraid of falling. Low impact exercise such as walking and aquatic aerobics improves strength, joint function and fitness without heavy joint loading, and water supports body weight so the fall risk during exercise is minimal. It keeps her active safely, which is exactly what she asked for.
why_wrong_block:
A. Static stretching helps flexibility as an adjunct but does not build strength, balance or aerobic fitness, so on its own it neither keeps her active nor lowers fall risk.
C. High impact exercise (jumping, running) loads the arthritic joints and increases the risk of falls and injury; it suits young people without joint disease.
D. Discouraging exercise leads to deconditioning, stiffness and weaker muscles, which worsen OA symptoms and actually increase falls; exercise is first line OA management.
key_concept:
OA exercise rule: keep moving, low impact.
  • Best: walking, swimming, water aerobics, cycling
  • Add strengthening and balance work
  • Avoid: jumping, running
  • Never: advise rest or stopping activity
exam_pearl: "Afraid of falling" points to water based, low impact exercise, not to stopping exercise.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot variant under 1407 (top of p354); Arabic line in screenshot states the correct answer is B.

stem: A patient with chronic hepatitis C presents with ascites and abdominal pain. Ascitic fluid analysis shows a neutrophil count of 300 cells/mm³. What is the most appropriate management?
why_right: Chronic hepatitis C with ascites plus abdominal pain and an ascitic neutrophil count of 300 (above the 250 cells/mm³ threshold) is spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, even without high fever. SBP needs prompt empirical systemic antibiotics, classically IV ceftriaxone (a third generation cephalosporin), before culture results.
why_wrong_block:
B. Steroids treat severe alcoholic or autoimmune hepatitis; they do not treat infection and would worsen SBP.
C. Antiviral therapy for HCV is important long term but does nothing for the acute, potentially fatal peritonitis that must be treated now.
D. TIPS is for refractory ascites or variceal bleeding; it does not treat SBP and is avoided during active infection.
key_concept:
SBP: ascitic neutrophils ≥250 cells/mm³ in a patient with ascites.
  • Clinical: abdominal pain or tenderness, fever (may be mild or absent), encephalopathy
  • Typical organism: E. coli
  • Treatment: IV ceftriaxone (third generation cephalosporin)
  • Add IV albumin when creatinine or bilirubin is raised (reduces hepatorenal syndrome)
  • Prophylaxis after an episode: ciprofloxacin
exam_pearl: Neutrophils above 250 in ascitic fluid = treat as SBP with antibiotics, regardless of temperature.

stem: Old patient diabetic, admitted to ICU with pneumonia and sepsis. What is the most appropriate empiric therapy in addition to azithromycin?
why_right: This is severe community acquired pneumonia (ICU, sepsis) in an elderly diabetic, and the lead-in says "in addition to azithromycin". The standard regimen for admitted or ICU CAP is a beta-lactam such as ceftriaxone (covers pneumococcus and common gram-negatives) plus a macrolide (covers atypicals), so ceftriaxone completes the pair.
why_wrong_block:
A. Moxifloxacin is an alternative to the beta-lactam plus macrolide combination, not an add-on to azithromycin; adding it duplicates atypical coverage and adds QT risk. It is the choice when a single comorbid-CAP agent is asked for.
B. Vancomycin covers MRSA only and is added when there are MRSA risk factors (prior MRSA, recent IV antibiotics, post influenza necrotizing pneumonia); none is given here.
key_concept:
Empirical CAP therapy:
  • Healthy outpatient: macrolide (azithromycin)
  • Comorbid: respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) OR beta-lactam + macrolide
  • Admitted or ICU: ceftriaxone + azithromycin (or beta-lactam + fluoroquinolone)
  • MRSA risk: add vancomycin or linezolid
  • Pseudomonas risk or HAP: antipseudomonal beta-lactam (piperacillin/tazobactam, meropenem)
exam_pearl: Read the lead-in: "in addition to azithromycin" asks for the beta-lactam (ceftriaxone); a variant without that phrase asking for a single comorbid-CAP drug is keyed to moxifloxacin.

stem: Old in 50s or 60s KC of HTN and DM, signs of dehydration. Came complaining of severe vomiting and diarrhea. A week ago she had an appointment with her primary physician Cr was 60, now her creatinine is 160. The cause of kidney injury? Urine sodium 60, urine osmolality 220, specific gravity 900, BUN 11.
why_right: This recall's key is pre-renal azotemia because the story is volume loss: severe vomiting and diarrhea, signs of dehydration, and creatinine rising from 60 to 160 within a week in a previously stable patient. Hypovolemia reduces renal perfusion, and pre-renal AKI from dehydration is reversible with IV fluids; the recaller summarized the case as dehydration.
why_wrong_block:
B. Acute on chronic kidney injury needs evidence of pre-existing CKD; her baseline creatinine one week ago was normal (60), so there is no chronic disease to build on.
C. ATN is the intrinsic injury that follows prolonged or severe hypoperfusion (or nephrotoxins, contrast) and shows high urine sodium (above 40), low urine osmolality (below 300) and a FeNa above 2%; the recaller's summary pointed to simple dehydration.
key_concept:
Pre-renal vs intrinsic (ATN) AKI indices:
  • Urine sodium: pre-renal <20; ATN >40
  • FeNa: pre-renal <1%; ATN >2%
  • Urine osmolality: pre-renal >500 (concentrated); ATN <300
  • Specific gravity: pre-renal >1.010; ATN about 1.010 or less
  • BUN:creatinine: pre-renal >20:1
  • Diuretics can raise urine sodium even in pre-renal AKI
exam_pearl: History of fluid loss suggests pre-renal, but if urine sodium is high and urine is dilute, the injury has progressed to ATN.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Recaller notes the case was long with many labs; summary is that she was dehydrated; sure of the three options. Typed recall lists 'A. Pre renal azotemia' as the answer.

stem: A 28-year-old man who recently joined military service and underwent excessive military training presents to the Emergency Department with lightheadedness on standing and fatigue. Physical examination reveals postural hypotension, otherwise unremarkable. Urine osmolality is elevated >500 mOsm/kg. What is the most likely etiology for his acute kidney injury?
why_right: Excessive military training causes volume loss, and postural hypotension confirms hypovolemia. A urine osmolality > 500 means the tubules are intact and concentrating urine maximally, which defines pre-renal azotemia.
why_wrong_block:
B. AIN is intrinsic renal injury; damaged tubules cannot concentrate, so urine osmolality is low (< 300), and it usually follows a drug.
C. Glomerulonephritis is intrinsic renal disease with hematuria, RBC casts, edema and hypertension rather than postural hypotension.
D. ATN can follow prolonged hypovolemia, but tubular damage gives dilute urine (< 300) and FeNa > 2%; a concentrated urine means the tubules still work.
key_concept:
Pre-renal vs intrinsic AKI indices:
  • Urine osmolality: > 500 pre-renal; < 300 intrinsic
  • FeNa: < 1% pre-renal; > 2% ATN
  • Urine Na: low pre-renal; high ATN
  • BUN:Cr: > 20 pre-renal
  • Sediment: bland pre-renal; muddy brown casts ATN
exam_pearl: Concentrated urine (> 500) = tubules working = pre-renal; if exertion also gave dark urine and high CK, think rhabdomyolysis.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 3× in this file (also AS-0004, AS-2501).
Compiler note: Unnumbered related question placed under 1417.

stem: A 16-year-old man presented to the Outpatient Department complaining of diarrhea for 3 years. He was passing 3-4 large volumes of stool per day, which was foul smelling and contained undigested food but no blood or mucus. He was also complaining of postprandial bloating and easy fatigability. On examination, he looked pale and has no secondary sexual characteristics, BMI 14 kg/m2. Hb 10 (130-170 g/L), MCV 70 (80-95), platelets 433 (150-400 x 10^9/L), ALT 90 (5-40 IU/L), AST 60 (12-40 IU/L), ESR 12 (2-10 mm/h). Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic test?
why_right: A 16-year-old with 3 years of large, foul smelling stools with undigested food (malabsorption), bloating, BMI 14, no secondary sexual characteristics (delayed puberty), microcytic anemia (iron malabsorption) and mildly raised transaminases is a classic picture of celiac disease. The appropriate diagnostic test among the options is celiac serology, IgA anti-endomysial antibodies, followed by duodenal biopsy for confirmation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Fecal fat confirms steatorrhea but cannot tell which malabsorptive disease is responsible, so it does not make the diagnosis.
B. Barium follow through is nonspecific imaging used mainly for small bowel Crohn disease (strictures, fistulae); there is no blood or mucus and the ESR is only trivially raised, so Crohn is not suggested and it cannot diagnose celiac disease.
C. The lactose breath test diagnoses lactose intolerance, which causes bloating and diarrhea but not growth failure, delayed puberty or iron deficiency anemia.
key_concept:
Celiac disease workup:
  • Clues: chronic diarrhea, bloating, weight loss, low BMI, iron deficiency anemia, raised transaminases, short stature or delayed puberty
  • Associations: type 1 diabetes, dermatitis herpetiformis
  • Initial serology: IgA tTG (with total IgA); EMA is the alternative serology
  • Confirm: duodenal biopsy (villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, intraepithelial lymphocytes)
  • Treatment: gluten free diet; follow compliance with tTG
exam_pearl: If tTG is not among the options, anti-endomysial antibody is the celiac serology to choose.

stem: A 40-year-old man presented to the emergency department with fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia for two days. On physical examination, the physician asked the patient to flex his neck forward. This maneuver caused involuntary flexion of the patient hips and knees. Which of the following clinical signs is demonstrated in this patient?
highlight_terms_source: involuntary flexion of the patient hips and knees
why_right: In a patient with meningitis features (fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia), passive flexion of the neck that produces involuntary flexion of the hips and knees is the Brudzinski (neck) sign. It reflects meningeal irritation: stretching the inflamed meninges triggers reflex flexion of the lower limbs.
why_wrong_block:
A. Kernig sign is elicited with the hip flexed to 90 degrees: extending the knee is resisted or painful. It tests the legs, not neck flexion.
B. Babinski sign is an upgoing big toe on stroking the sole, indicating an upper motor neuron lesion; it is not a meningeal sign.
D. Romberg sign is loss of balance on standing with feet together and eyes closed, indicating sensory (proprioceptive) ataxia from dorsal column or peripheral nerve disease.
key_concept:
Bedside signs:
  • Brudzinski: neck flexion causes hip and knee flexion (meningism)
  • Kernig: hip flexed 90, knee extension painful or resisted (meningism)
  • Babinski: upgoing plantar (UMN lesion)
  • Romberg: falls with eyes closed (sensory ataxia)
  • Meningeal signs have low sensitivity; a negative sign does not exclude meningitis
exam_pearl: Brudzinski = Bend the neck (legs flex); Kernig = Knee extension (hip flexed).

stem: How long should H. pylori triple therapy be used:
why_right: H. pylori eradication regimens (PPI plus two antibiotics, classically amoxicillin and clarithromycin) are short antibiotic courses given for 7 to 14 days. The question asks for the duration of triple therapy, which is a course measured in days, not weeks or months.
why_wrong_block:
B. Three months is far longer than any eradication course; prolonged antibiotics add side effects and resistance without benefit. Long courses belong to things like TB therapy, not H. pylori.
C. Four weeks is the interval to wait after finishing antibiotics before retesting for eradication (urea breath test), not the treatment duration. A PPI may be continued longer to heal an ulcer, but the triple therapy itself is not 4 weeks.
key_concept:
H. pylori: treat with a short antibiotic course, then confirm eradication.
  • First line: PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin for 7 to 14 days
  • Failure: quadruple therapy (PPI + bismuth + metronidazole + tetracycline)
  • Test of cure: urea breath test, at least 4 weeks after antibiotics
  • Stop PPI about 2 weeks before the breath test to avoid false negatives
exam_pearl: Do not confuse the 4 week wait before retesting with the 7 to 14 day treatment course; current practice favours the full 14 days.

stem: Persistent HTN , FH OF STROKE , potassium 3,2 , muscle proximal 4/5 what test to reach diagnosis ?
key_concept:
Hypertension + low K: decide between aldosterone excess and cortisol excess by the body habitus.
  • No Cushingoid features: aldosterone:renin ratio (Conn)
  • Obesity, striae, diabetes, bruising: 24 h urine free cortisol, late night salivary cortisol or 1 mg dexamethasone test
  • Both can cause hypokalemia and proximal weakness
  • Familial early stroke + hyperaldosteronism: glucocorticoid remediable aldosteronism
exam_pearl: Proximal weakness alone does not mean Cushing: hypokalemia itself causes muscle weakness, so look for the Cushingoid body features.
